text: Kestrel, ARES Control. You are go for powered descent. Winds two metres per second from the north-west.
Copy, Control. Kestrel is go. I can see the crater rim.
That's Jezero. Forty-five kilometres wide. A lake filled it three and a half billion years ago.
Welcome to Mars, {0}. Watch your fuel: gravity here is only 38% of Earth's, but there's almost no air to slow you down.
Throttling up. Altitude two hundred.
Contact light... touchdown. Kestrel, you are on Mars.
{0}, this is Commander Reyes. Before you take a single step, run the suit check at the lander's suit port.
Then walk to the landing beacon and come up to the habitat. I'll meet you there.
Airlock cycling. Pressure coming up to seventy kilopascals... There. You can take your helmet off.
This is home: four modules, eleven people, and a wall twenty centimetres thick between us and a vacuum-cold desert.
Find me at the command terminal outside when you've stretched your legs. The colony board will tell you more than I can.
There you are. Maya Reyes. I run this place, or try to.
Systems engineer {0}, reporting. Callsign {1}.
Good. We needed you yesterday. The last dust storm left scars everywhere, and Earth is three to twenty-two light-minutes away.
Out here, if something breaks, nobody is coming. There's just us.
Check the colony dashboard at the command terminal. Learn what keeps us alive. Then we get to work.
You've seen the numbers. Power is the problem behind every other problem.
Get some rest, {0}. Tomorrow we start with the solar farm.
Commander, battery bank at eighteen percent and falling. The storm buried half the solar farm.
{0}, we're going into emergency power mode. Non-essential systems are off as of now.
Get to the solar farm east of the colony. Find out what the storm did to it.
Thank you. The seedlings wouldn't have survived another cold night without the lamps.
The spectrograph thanks you. Amara won't, but I'll buy her a coffee.
Elias, lettuce can't drink coffee.
Good call. Water is the one thing we can never run short of. Amara will forgive us, eventually.
Batteries are charging. The lights stay on tonight.
Remember what you chose today. Every watt on Mars is a decision about who gets it.
This is Nara Erdene, life support. Oxygen output is down sixty percent and I don't know why yet.
Meet me at the oxygen plant. Bring your eyes and your patience.
So you're the new engineer. Reyes says you're good. We'll see.
This plant breathes Martian air: ninety-five percent carbon dioxide. Heat it to eight hundred degrees, push it through a ceramic cell, and the cell strips off oxygen.
Same principle as MOXIE on Perseverance?
The same, scaled up four thousand times. Start at the intake tower. Read the instruments before you touch anything.
The filter design failed in its first big storm. The ISA engineers on Earth will want a full report.
Or we redesign it ourselves. It's our air. What do you think?
Report it to Earth. Other colonies use the same filter.
We fix it here. By the time Earth answers, we'll have built three prototypes.
Fair. Somebody on Titan Station will breathe easier because of it.
Now you're talking like a Martian.
Purity ninety-nine point six percent, flow back to rated. The habitat is breathing on its own again.
Good work, both of you. Nara doesn't hand out compliments, {0}. Take that as one.
Water reserves are at eighteen hundred kilos. That's six weeks if nothing else goes wrong.
Come and see me. I found something in the old archives.
Before ARES-1 there was Ares-0, the first expedition, in 2161. They ran an ice survey a few hundred metres north-west of here.
Their station lost power in 2163 and nobody ever went back for the data.
If they mapped the ground ice, we don't have to drill blind. Find the station and pull its data core.
And watch your oxygen. It's a long walk.
The data core is intact! Three candidate ice sites around the station.
Scan all three with the ground-penetrating radar, then choose the best one at the station console.
Ares-0 log, Commander Tomas Halvorsen, sol 412. The storm took our main array. The crew leaves the survey station tomorrow.
For whoever finds this: the ice under site B is the real thing. Sixty percent water, a metre down.
One more thing. Our gravimeter keeps logging a tiny pull from the outer Solar System that no planet explains. Control classified the data. Code: HALVORSEN-2161.
If you're hearing this, the colony made it. Good. Tell Maya she was right: the ice was here all along.
Twenty-five hundred kilos and climbing. The tanks sound different when they're full.
Ares-0 died for lack of water. We won't.
Amara Okafor, greenhouse. Our pumps failed overnight and the plants have stopped growing.
Please come quickly. They can't wait the way people can.
Every plant in here is a tiny life-support machine: it drinks light, breathes our carbon dioxide and gives back oxygen and food.
Hydroponics means no soil. The roots sit in a film of water carrying every nutrient they need.
Martian regolith is full of perchlorates, so for now this is the only way we eat.
Fix the pumps first. Then we'll tune nutrients, light and climate together.
First harvest of the season. It's a small basket, but it's ours.
Thank you, {0}. You fed eleven people today.
We're losing water faster than we drink it. Twelve percent of the loop is going missing.
Come to the recycling plant behind the habitat. On Mars, nothing is waste.
Every drop we drink has been drunk before: by us, by the plants, by the air.
The plant filters greywater, distils urine, and a bioreactor turns waste into fertiliser for Amara.
Find where the loop leaks, fix it, then make it efficient without touching life support.
Ninety-seven percent recovery. That's better than the old ISS ever managed.
And my plants get their nitrogen back. Nara, I'll admit it: you're a genius.
{0}, I need you at the habitat. Not for a repair this time.
People are arguing, and I'd rather they argue in a council than in the corridors.
Two camps are forming. Some want ARES-1 to govern itself. Others say the International Space Authority built this place and should keep running it.
Neither side is wrong. Earth paid for every bolt. But Earth can't answer a call for twenty minutes.
Before the council meets, help where people need it: the residential air handlers, Jun's comms dispute, and Lena's medical bay.
People listen to the ones who fix things.
The ISA wants all our traffic to go through their licensed relay. Every message, every data packet.
I want to build our own relay so we're never cut off again. They call that a breach of contract.
You're neutral. What should I do?
Build the independent relay.
Follow the ISA's rules.
Ask the ISA to approve a backup relay.
Then that's what I'll do. If the ISA complains, they can call me. In twenty minutes.
You're probably right. I hate it, but you're probably right.
A backup they sign off on. Huh. Why didn't I think of that?
Oh good, the supplies. Two of the night shift have radiation burns from the storm EVA.
Mars doesn't hurt you all at once. It's cosmic rays, cold and dust in your lungs, a little every day.
Thank you, {0}. Tell the council that healthy colonists matter more than flags.
This council will decide where ARES-1 puts its effort for the next ten years.
Self-sufficiency. Every greenhouse and every litre made here. Then nobody can switch us off.
Science. We're the best observatory site humans have ever had, and something strange is out there.
Cooperation with Earth. Their rockets, their data, our skills. We're stronger connected.
{0}, you've worked with all of them. The council will follow your recommendation.
Self-sufficiency: make ARES-1 independent.
Partnership with Earth: grow together with the ISA.
Science: lead humanity's research beyond Mars.
Self-sufficiency it is. I'll tell the ISA ourselves, before they hear it from someone else.
Partnership. Good. I'll start the call. They'll hear it in twelve minutes.
Science, then. Elias will be impossible to live with for a week.
The council has spoken. Whatever happens next, we decided it together.
{0}, it's Elias Chen, astrophysics. Olympus Observatory, our telescope in orbit, went silent three days ago.
Its last upload showed something impossible. Come to the comms dish.
Olympus watches two million stars for tiny changes. Two weeks ago, stars in one patch of sky brightened and faded, one after another.
Same shape every time, same in every colour. That's the signature of gravitational lensing: a mass passing in front of them.
But there's nothing there. No light at all. And then the observatory went dark.
Take the lander to orbit, bring Olympus back, and recover its archive.
A mass of about six Earths, at the edge of the Solar System, and completely dark.
And the archive mentions a name I haven't heard in eighteen years: PROJECT HORIZON.
{0}, it's Jun. While you were in orbit, the dish caught something buried in the noise. A transmission, eighteen years old.
It carries a PROJECT HORIZON identifier.
Horizon was an ISA deep-space mission, launched from Mars orbit in 2171. Four crew. It went silent a year later. Officially: reactor failure.
The signal is weak and broken into pieces. I need your help filtering it at the Observatory console.
If Horizon was chasing the same dark mass, their data could tell us what it is.
There's also an old ISA data relay still in Mars orbit. If anything reached home, it's there.
Horizon, mission day 203. Commander Ilse Varga. Target acquired by lensing. Mass estimate: zero point six Earth masses. Proceeding to rendezvous.
Day 288. The target pulls harder than predicted. Navigation is recalculating. Something is wrong with our mass estimate.
Day 291. Flyby complete, but we were thrown far off course. We can't brake. We're putting the instrument pods into orbit while we still can.
Day 296. There is a second signal under the first. Repeat: a second signal. Transmitting everything to the relay.
Horizon's archive is decoded. Six Earth masses, a few centimetres across. That isn't a planet.
Earth will want this immediately. Some here want to verify it ourselves first, before anyone else tells the story. What do you think?
Send everything to Earth now.
Verify it here first, then share.
Sending it now. Whatever the ISA knew before, they'll know we know.
We'll check every number twice. When we speak, nobody will be able to argue with it.
With Horizon's measurements we can rebuild the object in a simulation.
I'm opening the Black Hole Research Laboratory. Because that's what I think it is.
The laboratory is ready. Open it from the Observatory console by the comms dish.
We'll rebuild HORIZON-1 from its numbers and see if it behaves like a black hole.
Set the mass to six Earth masses, that's 1.8 times ten to the minus five suns. Then give it some spin and thin out the disk; there's hardly any gas out there.
Orbit the camera around it and line up a background star until you see the ring. Then we chase the signal.
A primordial black hole. Formed in the first second after the Big Bang, with the mass of six Earths and the size of a grapefruit.
It's been drifting at the edge of our Solar System for billions of years, spinning at eighty percent of the maximum.
Horizon found it first. Now we know why their navigation failed.
{0}, come to the command terminal. We have a decision to make.
Horizon's pods are still out there, still recording. Somebody has to go and get them.
The ISA has approved an expedition. One ship, four crew, twenty-two months each way. I want you on it.
You'll prepare the ship: upgrades, life support, navigation. The same three things that failed Horizon.
Ilse Varga and I were in the same astronaut class. She was the best of us.
Bring her data home, {0}. And bring yourself home too.
Twenty-two months, {0}. Welcome to the edge of the Solar System. HORIZON-1 is right in front of you, and you can't see it.
Only the stars around it are bent. Look for the pods' beacons: they blink every forty seconds. Tab through the targets.
Final log. Ilse Varga, day 301. The pods are in stable orbits, far outside the danger zone. They'll keep watching for decades.
We're on an escape trajectory. No fuel to turn back. My crew knew the risk, and they chose the data.
The second signal is real. HORIZON-1 has a companion: two black holes, circling each other.
Whoever finds this: finish our work. And tell Maya Reyes the coffee is on me.
Olympus is back online, and the Observatory console by the dish can task it now. I've queued a few targets if you're curious.
Dust storm front from the south, arriving within a sol and a half.
{0}: batteries above seventy percent and clean panels, before the sky goes dark.
Pressure alarm in module three! A slow leak at a seal. Patch it before we lose too much air.
Rafael Ortiz, chief mechanic. Pleasure. Want to see a sad rover?
Rosa froze during the storm and won't wake up. The battery reads full, the motors won't turn.
You've got fresh eyes. Run a diagnosis on her, and if you find it, fix it. I'll owe you a real coffee.
Embarrassing request: I lost a data drive with two years of observation notes near the Perseverance rover.
It's a museum piece now, but I go there to think. Could you look for it?
You found it! Two years of spectra. Thank you.
Have a look at what's on it. It's mostly stars, but stars are mostly what I love.
My dwarf-wheat trial is turning yellow and I can't work out why.
Could you check the test bed? I'm too close to it. I've stared at those leaves for a week.
Iron locked out by high pH. Of course! I've been chasing a disease that didn't exist.
You've saved six months of work. I owe you a loaf of Martian bread.
Small favour: Tomas in module two can't call his daughter on Earth. His antenna feed died in the storm.
Could you fix the feed on the habitat mast and test the link at the command terminal?
{0}, the dish keeps slewing on its own at night, pointing at nothing. Can you check the drive?
An unregistered relay in high orbit, bouncing encrypted bursts off our dish. ISA cipher.
Somebody has been listening to us, or talking past us, for years.
I'll keep a copy. Quietly.
You went to the Ares-0 site.
Tomas Halvorsen commanded it. I was the youngest of his crew. He stayed behind so the three of us could make the last launch home.
Thank you for going. I've never been able to.
Every morning I check three numbers: oxygen, water, power. Everything else is commentary.
If you need anything, ask. If you break anything, tell me first.
The colony feels different lately. People talk about "us" and "Earth" as if they were separate places.
My job is to keep everyone alive long enough to disagree.
When Horizon launched, half the colony watched from the pad. I was one of them.
Whatever is out there, I want everyone who goes to come back.
From Mars the sky is darker than any desert on Earth. I can see other galaxies with my own eyes.
Sunlight takes thirteen minutes to reach us. Everything you see in the sky is the past.
Olympus sends me two terabytes a night. I read the interesting parts over breakfast.
Amara thinks I'm married to the telescope. She's not wrong.
Six Earth masses in a sphere you could hold in two hands. I still can't quite believe it.
Every black hole bends light the same way. Understand one and you understand them all.
My grandmother raised horses in Arkhangai. She said the land gives back what you take care of. Mars is the same.
Breathe in, thank the oxygen plant. Breathe out, thank the scrubber.
Closed loops are beautiful. Nothing leaves, nothing is wasted. Like a ger: everything has its place.
Amara and I argue about water every day. That's how we know we both care.
If Horizon was lost to a wrong number, then the numbers matter more than anything.
Whatever the council decides, the air still has to be made every morning.
Plants are honest. If something's wrong, they show you within a day.
My first garden was a window box in Lagos. Now it's the only farm on a planet.
The plants give us more oxygen than you'd think. Not enough to live on, but enough to notice.
Taste this tomato. That's what home tastes like, even here.
If you find Horizon's logs, bring back the crew's names. Names matter.
I've started a seed bank. Whatever happens, something will grow.
Every message to Earth waits in a queue. Birthdays, reports, love letters, all in order.
The dish is older than I am. I talk to it. It mostly listens.
Twelve minutes each way. You learn to say everything in one go.
Some nights I just listen to the noise between the stars. It's very calming. Mostly.
Horizon's signal sat in our archives for eighteen years and nobody noticed. I keep thinking about that.
Whatever you find out there, I'll make sure all of Mars hears it.
On Earth I fixed tractors. On Mars I fix everything. Same thing, more dust.
Rosa? My rover. Every machine deserves a name.
Dust gets into everything. Seals, bearings, coffee.
The trick with machines out here: listen before you open them.
They're building the expedition ship in my workshop. Best thing I've ever worked on.
If the navigation computer gives you trouble, kick it. Gently. It's tradition.
Drink water, wear your dosimeter and come and see me if you feel strange. In that order.
In low gravity, bones lose about one percent of their density a month. Exercise isn't optional here.
People think the danger is a broken suit. Usually it's loneliness.
Every colonist gets a check-up after a storm. Yes, including you.
Twenty-two months in deep space is a lot of radiation. The shielding matters.
Come back healthy. That's an order. Well, a medical recommendation.
The lamps were off for three sols. I lost two trays of seedlings.
I understand why you did it. I just needed you to know what it cost.
You found Tomas's last recording. He said I was right about the ice.
We argued about it the night before we left. I never got to hear him admit it. Thank you.
Since the council chose self-sufficiency, people walk differently. As if the place is theirs.
Now we have to prove we can keep it.
The council chose science, and now the whole colony is asking me questions. I love it.
Ask me anything. Really, anything.
With the partnership, the ISA is sending a new relay and better data. We're not alone out here.
It turns out cooperation needs good antennas.
Our own relay is up. No more asking permission to call home.
The ISA sent a strongly worded letter. It took twelve minutes to arrive. I framed it.
Earth has the Horizon data. The ISA called back within a day. That's a record.
They're not happy about the questions we're asking. Good.
We checked everything twice before telling Earth. Nobody could argue with a single number.
Elias says it's the best paper this colony will ever write.
The expedition came home to a colony that no longer waited for supply ships.
ARES-1 grew from eleven people to three hundred. Its greenhouses fed them all; its recyclers wasted nothing.
Children were born who had never seen Earth, and did not miss it.
The council kept meeting, kept arguing, and kept deciding together.
HORIZON-1's data went into the archive. One day, someone would use it.
But that was for later. For now, Mars was enough.
Humanity had a second home.
The recovered pods reached Earth, and with them a question: what else lies at the edge of the Solar System?
ARES-1 became a harbour. Ships were built in its orbit, crewed by people born under a butterscotch sky.
Within ten years, outposts circled Jupiter's moons and the first station kept watch over HORIZON-1.
The route Horizon could not survive became a highway, with navigation that weighed everything it passed.
Mars was no longer the frontier. It was the place you set out from.
And every ship that left carried Commander Varga's name on its hull.
Humanity had stepped beyond the red planet.
Eighteen years of pod data changed physics.
HORIZON-1 and its companion were the first primordial black holes ever confirmed: relics of the universe's first second.
If they existed here, they could exist everywhere. Astronomers began to suspect they were part of the dark matter that holds galaxies together.
The binary's slow dance was measured to a precision Einstein never imagined, and his equations held.
The discovery was named the Varga Binary, after the commander who heard the second signal first.
At ARES-1, Dr. Elias Chen opened a school. Its first lesson was how to find something that gives off no light.
The Horizon Project was complete. Its questions were only beginning.
The ERGOSPHERE files went out on every channel ARES-1 had.
The worlds learned that the ISA had known about HORIZON-1 for thirteen years, and why it had kept the secret.
A spinning black hole at the edge of the Solar System: an energy source that could outlast the Sun, or a prize worth any war.
There were investigations, resignations, and for a while, anger.
Then, slowly, something else: an agreement, signed by every nation on both worlds, that HORIZON-1 belongs to no one.
Beyond Neptune, two small black holes kept circling, as they had since the universe was a second old.
Some horizons are meant to be crossed together.
Commander Maya Reyes led ARES-1 for another twelve years. She finally visited the Ares-0 site and left a crew patch on the hatch.
Nara Erdene designed ARES-1's next life-support plant herself. It never needed a single part from Earth.
Nara Erdene trained a new generation of life-support engineers. She called them her herd.
Amara Okafor's seed bank grew to two thousand varieties. The first Mars-bred wheat carries her name.
Amara Okafor never forgot the sols the lamps went dark. Her new greenhouse got its own power plant.
Elias Chen spent the rest of his life studying the Varga Binary, and never once missed his breakfast reading.
Elias Chen went back to his stars, with two new ones in his notebook that give off no light at all.
Jun Park's independent relay never dropped a call. Mars could always hear itself.
Jun Park became the ISA's chief of communications on Mars, and rewrote the rules he had once followed.
Jun Park's approved backup relay became the model for every colony after ARES-1.
The crew of Horizon, Ilse Varga, Kofi Mensah, Ana Lindqvist and Hiro Tanaka, are remembered on a plaque at Olympus Observatory. Their pods are still watching.
And {0}, callsign {1}, came home. Not a hero, as they always said. Just the engineer who kept a fragile world alive.
